claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results in relation to the two models presented in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Optogenetically inhibiting neck muscles prevented waves generated in the head from propagating through the neck in most trials.
claims.source: In most trials, optogenetically inhibiting neck muscles prevented waves generated in the head from propagating through the neck.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments.

claims.claim: During the interruption of head waves by neck muscle inhibition, the tail exhibited bending undulations at a higher frequency than that of the head, resulting in two-frequency undulation (2FU).
claims.source: During the interruption of these waves, the tail exhibited bending undulations at a higher frequency than that of the head, resulting in the animal simultaneously undulating at two distinct frequencies (Figure 3A, Video 2). We henceforth refer to this behavior, whether or not induced by any manipulation, as two-frequency undulation (2FU).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Video 2.

claims.claim: 2FU was observed upon inhibiting all neck cholinergic neurons.
claims.source: We observed 2FU upon inhibiting all neck cholinergic neurons (Figure 3B, Video 2) and also upon inhibiting neck B-type motor neurons (Pacr-5::Arch; Figure 3C, Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and Video 2.

claims.claim: 2FU was observed upon inhibiting neck B-type motor neurons.
claims.source: We observed 2FU upon inhibiting all neck cholinergic neurons (Figure 3B, Video 2) and also upon inhibiting neck B-type motor neurons (Pacr-5::Arch; Figure 3C, Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and Video 2.

claims.claim: These manipulations led to a large decrease in wave amplitude in the neck and a smaller decrease in wave amplitude in the tail.
claims.source: These manipulations led to a large decrease in wave amplitude in the neck and a smaller decrease in wave amplitude in the tail (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Multiple animals in each experiment showed 2FU, with the highest ratios of tail frequency to head frequency seen in worms in which the neck muscles were inhibited.
claims.source: Nevertheless, multiple animals in each experiment showed 2FU, with the highest ratios of tail frequency to head frequency seen in worms in which the neck muscles were inhibited (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The bending amplitude of the tail generally decreased as the frequency increased.
claims.source: The bending amplitude of the tail generally decreased as the frequency increased (Figure 3E,F), consistent with the changes in bending frequency and amplitude previously observed when the viscosity of a fluid environment was varied (Fang-Yen et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E and 3F, and is consistent with previous findings cited.

claims.claim: The opposite trends of amplitude and frequency may reflect a constraint to the maximum absolute rate of change of curvature, which is proportional to the product of amplitude and frequency.
claims.source: The opposite trends of amplitude and frequency may reflect a constraint to the maximum absolute rate of change of curvature, which is proportional to the product of amplitude and frequency.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed relationship between amplitude and frequency.

claims.claim: Lesioning mid-body muscles in Pmyo-3::PH::miniSOG worms led to stronger decoupling between head and tail oscillations, but did not prevent 2FU.
claims.source: To test whether 2FU can occur after stronger disruption of motor coupling, we lesioned mid-body muscles in Pmyo-3::PH::miniSOG worms. This manipulation indeed led to stronger decoupling between head and tail oscillations, but did still not prevent 2FU (Figure 3D, Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and Video 2.

claims.claim: Selective activation of small portions of the tail motor circuit while inhibiting the rest led to high-frequency localized undulations in the tail in several animals.
claims.source: We therefore examined worms in which both the inhibitory opsin NpHR and the excitatory opsin Channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) were expressed in the cholinergic neurons, after the A-type motor neurons were ablated by Punc-4::miniSOG. We first illuminated these animals with 590 nm wavelength (yellow) light throughout the body to inhibit all cholinergic neurons. While maintaining this yellow illumination, we targeted small portions of the tail with 473 nm wavelength (blue) light, activating ChR2 and stimulating a few posterior B and AS neurons. Under these conditions, several animals generated high-frequency localized undulations in the tail (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Video 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Video 3.

claims.claim: Independent head and tail oscillations were observed in animals without induced lesions or optogenetic perturbations when transitioning between regions of different viscosities.
claims.source: When we studied worms transitioning between regions of a low-viscosity buffer into highly viscoelastic hydroxypropylmethylcellulose (HPMC) islands (see Methods), we observed 2FU in 6 of 41 worms (15%). In these animals, the tail continued oscillating at a high frequency for at least two full cycles even as the head frequency was sharply reduced (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Video 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and Video 3.

claims.claim: 2FU can occur in C. elegans with no internal perturbations.
claims.source: Although these events were uncommon, they demonstrated that 2FU can occur in C. elegans with no internal perturbations.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of 2FU in worms transitioning between different viscosity environments.

claims.claim: The C. elegans forward motor circuit contains at least two units capable of independent rhythm generation.
claims.source: Taken together, these results strongly suggest that the C. elegans forward motor circuit contains at least two units capable of independent rhythm generation and that a partial breakdown in anterior proprioceptive coupling (for example by inhibiting neck BWMs) is sufficient to reveal the presence of the posterior oscillating unit(s).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the multiple experiments showing 2FU under various conditions.

claims.claim: A partial breakdown in anterior proprioceptive coupling is sufficient to reveal the presence of posterior oscillating unit(s).
claims.source: Taken together, these results strongly suggest that the C. elegans forward motor circuit contains at least two units capable of independent rhythm generation and that a partial breakdown in anterior proprioceptive coupling (for example by inhibiting neck BWMs) is sufficient to reveal the presence of the posterior oscillating unit(s).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing 2FU upon disruption of coupling.

claims.claim: Almost all chemical or electrical synaptic connections to the VNC motor neurons are made by the premotor interneuron classes AVB, PVC, AVA, AVD, and AVE.
claims.source: Almost all chemical or electrical synaptic connections to the VNC motor neurons are made by the premotor interneuron (IN) classes AVB, PVC, AVA, AVD, and AVE (White et al., 1986).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to White et al., 1986.

claims.claim: Laser ablation studies have indicated that AVB, and to a lesser degree PVC, are essential for normal forward locomotion.
claims.source: Laser ablation studies have indicated that AVB, and to a lesser degree PVC, are essential for normal forward locomotion (Chalfie et al., 1985), although rudimentary forward crawling is possible in their absence if the reverse-driving A motor neurons are also removed (Gao et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Chalfie et al., 1985 and Gao et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Rudimentary forward crawling is possible in the absence of AVB and PVC if the reverse-driving A motor neurons are also removed.
claims.source: Laser ablation studies have indicated that AVB, and to a lesser degree PVC, are essential for normal forward locomotion (Chalfie et al., 1985), although rudimentary forward crawling is possible in their absence if the reverse-driving A motor neurons are also removed (Gao et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Gao et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Both Pnmr-1::ICE and Pglr-1::ICE strains were capable of 2FU during optogenetic inhibition of neck muscles.
claims.source: We found that both strains were capable of 2FU during optogenetic inhibition of neck muscles (Figure 4A,E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A, 4E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, 1E.

claims.claim: 2FU does not require most premotor interneurons, including the forward locomotory interneurons PVC.
claims.source: This result demonstrates that 2FU does not require most premotor interneurons, including the forward locomotory interneurons neurons PVC.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that 2FU occurs in Pnmr-1::ICE and Pglr-1::ICE strains.

claims.claim: unc-7 and unc-9 worms were capable of 2FU.
claims.source: We found that both strains were capable of 2FU, although it appeared to occur less often than in PVC-ablated animals, and sometimes occurred prior to neck muscle inhibition (Figure 4B,E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E; Figure 4—figure supplement 5A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B, 4E, and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The UNC-7/UNC-9 gap junctions, including those between AVB and the B-type motor neurons, are not required for 2FU.
claims.source: This finding shows that the UNC-7/UNC-9 gap junctions, including those between AVB and the B-type motor neurons, are not required for 2FU.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that unc-7 and unc-9 mutants can exhibit 2FU.

claims.claim: After ablation of AVB, 2FU events were nearly diminished.
claims.source: When subjected to the same experiment as described above, 2FU events were nearly diminished. Very rarely we observed uncoupled undulation events that were not correlated with neck muscle inhibition (Figure 4—figure supplements 1B, E, 2 and 5C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 1B, 1E, 2, and 5C.

claims.claim: Most individual classes of premotor interneurons, including AVA, AVD, AVE, and PVC, are not essential for 2FU.
claims.source: Taken together, these results suggest that most individual classes of premotor interneurons, including AVA, AVD, AVE, and PVC, are not essential for 2FU. However, AVB may play a key role in activating the rhythm generator(s) to allow oscillation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the various ablation experiments.

claims.claim: AVB may play a key role in activating the rhythm generator(s) to allow oscillation.
claims.source: Taken together, these results suggest that most individual classes of premotor interneurons, including AVA, AVD, AVE, and PVC, are not essential for 2FU. However, AVB may play a key role in activating the rhythm generator(s) to allow oscillation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that AVB ablation nearly eliminates 2FU.

claims.claim: Ablating the A- and VC-type motor neurons with Punc-4::miniSOG did not prevent 2FU induced by neck paralysis during forward locomotion.
claims.source: We found that ablating the A- and VC-type motor neurons with a genetically targeted ROS generator (Punc-4::miniSOG) did not prevent 2FU induced by neck paralysis during forward locomotion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and 1E.

claims.claim: The A and VC motor neurons are not necessary for the posterior forward oscillator(s).
claims.source: This result supports the idea that the A and VC motor neurons are not necessary for the posterior forward oscillator(s).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that 2FU occurs without A and VC motor neurons.

claims.claim: Animals harboring an unc-49(e407) mutation were capable of 2FU during neck muscle paralysis.
claims.source: We found that animals harboring an unc-49(e407) mutation, while very slow swimmers, were nonetheless capable of 2FU during neck muscle paralysis (Figure 4D,E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claims.claim: 2FU occurred very rarely after ablating DB3, VB3, and VB4 or VB8 and VB9.
claims.source: 2FU was observed very rarely after ablating DB3, VB3, and VB4 or VB8 and VB9 (Figure 4C,F), although in both conditions there were additional instances of 2FU that occurred outside the time 3 s window used for frequency analysis (Fouad et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and 4F.

claims.claim: 2FU occurred repeatedly, although not commonly, in all other B motor neuron ablation conditions tested.
claims.source: 2FU occurred repeatedly, although not commonly, in all other conditions. (Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4F and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: In the presence of premotor interneurons, the B class motor neurons contribute to neck-paralysis induced 2FU, but no single member is essential for generating high-frequency tail rhythms during 2FU.
claims.source: Taken together, these results suggest that in the presence of premotor interneurons, the B class motor neurons contribute to neck-paralysis induced 2FU, but no single member is essential for generating high-frequency tail rhythms during 2FU.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the various B motor neuron ablation experiments.

claims.claim: The A, VC and D motor neurons are not required for 2FU.
claims.source: The A, VC and D motor neurons are not required for 2FU.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ablation experiments.

claims.claim: Posterior rhythm generation can arise from multiple subsets of B or AS motor neurons.
claims.source: Our results are consistent with a model in which posterior rhythm generation can arise from multiple subsets of B or AS motor neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative model consistent with the experimental results.

claims.claim: vab-7 mutants had mildly or strongly paralyzed tails and were incapable of 2FU when neck muscles were inhibited.
claims.source: We found that vab-7 mutants had mildly or strongly paralyzed tails and were incapable of 2FU when neck muscles were inhibited, suggesting that vab-7 is essential for 2FU (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and 1E.

claims.claim: vab-7 is essential for 2FU.
claims.source: We found that vab-7 mutants had mildly or strongly paralyzed tails and were incapable of 2FU when neck muscles were inhibited, suggesting that vab-7 is essential for 2FU (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that vab-7 mutants cannot perform 2FU.

claims.claim: Worms in which most DB motor neurons were eliminated were dramatically less likely to show 2FU than mock controls, but were not incapable of doing so.
claims.source: Worms in which most DB motor neurons were eliminated were dramatically less likely to show 2FU than mock controls, but were not incapable of doing so (Figure 5, Video 4; N = 9 out of 104 trials from 25 worms by blinded, randomized scoring).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5 and Video 4.

claims.claim: Elimination of most VB motor neurons sharply reduced but did not eliminate the incidence of 2FU.
claims.source: We performed the converse experiment – elimination of most VB motor neurons using our infrared laser system – and found the incidence of 2FU was again sharply reduced but not eliminated (Figure 5, Video 4, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5, Video 4, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: When both DB and most VB motor neurons were removed, animals were incapable of 2FU.
claims.source: When we combined miniSOG and laser ablation to remove all DB and most VB motor neurons, animals were incapable of 2FU (Figure 5; 0 out of 102 trials from 27 worms by blinded, randomized scoring).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The B motor neurons as a class are essential for independent tail undulation during forward movement.
claims.source: Taken together, these results suggest that the B motor neurons as a class are essential for independent tail undulation during forward movement.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that removal of both DB and VB eliminates 2FU.

claims.claim: The B motor neurons have a role in generating the high-frequency locomotory rhythm observed in 2FU.
claims.source: Our results are consistent with the hypothesis that the B motor neurons have a role in generating the high-frequency locomotory rhythm observed in 2FU.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis consistent with the experimental results.

claims.claim: Severing both the VNC and the dorsal nerve cord (DNC) just posterior to the pharynx eliminated synaptic connections between the mid-body motor neurons and the head circuits.
claims.source: To ascertain whether the mid-body motor circuit is capable of independent rhythm generation, we developed a method for eliminating synaptic connections between the mid-body motor neurons and the head circuits. We used our infrared laser system to sever both the VNC and the dorsal nerve cord (DNC) just posterior to the pharynx.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used.

claims.claim: In many cases, severing the VNC and DNC also severed other fasciculated process bundles that run parallel to the VNC and DNC.
claims.source: In many cases, this procedure also severed other fasciculated process bundles that run parallel to the VNC and DNC (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Most animals were inactive several hours after disruption of the nerve cords, but active forward locomotion was induced by application of a mechanical stimulus.
claims.source: Several hours after disruption of the nerve cords, most animals were inactive (data not shown), but active forward locomotion was induced by application of a mechanical stimulus.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments.

claims.claim: Most worms with severed VNC and DNC could generate robust oscillations posterior to the cut location.
claims.source: Most of these worms could generate robust oscillations posterior to the cut location (Figure 6A,E, Video 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A, 6E, and Video 5.

claims.claim: The tail often undulated at a higher frequency than the mid-body in worms with severed VNC and DNC.
claims.source: Moreover, the tail often undulated at a higher frequency than the mid-body (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: In some cases, low-amplitude waves propagating in the posterior-to-anterior direction occurred simultaneously with robust mid-body and tail waves propagating in the anterior-to-posterior direction.
claims.source: In some cases, low-amplitude waves propagating in the posterior-to-anterior direction occurred simultaneously with robust mid-body and tail waves propagating in the anterior-to-posterior direction (Figure 6A, Video 5), suggesting a deficit in coordination between circuits on either side of the lesion.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A and Video 5.

claims.claim: Synaptic connections from the head circuits to the motor neurons may not be essential for wave generation posterior to the head.
claims.source: These results suggest that synaptic connections from the head circuits to the motor neurons may not be essential for wave generation posterior to the head.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that oscillations occur posterior to VNC/DNC cuts.

claims.claim: VNC-lesioned worms exhibited very little movement in the head but continued to generate robust oscillations in the mid-body and even higher frequency oscillations in the tail.
claims.source: Animals treated with these three lesions are henceforth referred to as 'VNC-lesioned' worms. These worms exhibited very little movement in the head. However, they continued to generate robust oscillations in the mid-body and even higher frequency oscillations in the tail (Figure 6B,E, Video 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B, 6E, and Video 5.

claims.claim: The pattern of locomotion in VNC-lesioned animals strongly resembled the 2FU induced by optogenetic perturbation, with the important difference that in the lesioned preparation, both frequencies were likely generated outside the head.
claims.source: The pattern of locomotion in VNC-lesioned animals strongly resembled the 2FU induced by optogenetic perturbation, with the important difference that in our lesioned preparation, both frequencies were likely generated outside the head.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the VNC-lesioned results to the optogenetic 2FU results.

claims.claim: The VNC motor circuit itself may contain multiple units capable of independent oscillation.
claims.source: The emergence of multiple frequencies of undulation outside the head suggests that the VNC motor circuit itself may contain multiple units capable of independent oscillation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of multiple frequencies in VNC-lesioned worms.

claims.claim: When the VNC and DNC were cut in two locations (in the neck and in the tail), animals could generate robust body oscillations posterior to the first cut and higher frequency oscillations posterior to the second cut.
claims.source: To test this possibility directly, we cut the VNC and DNC in two locations: in the neck (anterior to VB3) and in the tail (posterior to VB8). We again thermally lesioned the head neurons to suppress head movement. Under these conditions, the VNC motor neurons between VB3 and VB8 are isolated from circuitry in both the head and tail, and the VNC motor neurons posterior to VB8 are isolated from both the head circuits and the anterior VNC motor neurons. As before, these animals could generate robust body oscillations posterior to the first cut and higher frequency oscillations posterior to the second cut (Figure 6C,E, Video 5), suggesting that rhythms can arise independently from each of these portions of the VNC motor neurons.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C, 6E, and Video 5.

claims.claim: Rhythms can arise independently from multiple portions of the VNC motor neurons.
claims.source: As before, these animals could generate robust body oscillations posterior to the first cut and higher frequency oscillations posterior to the second cut (Figure 6C,E, Video 5), suggesting that rhythms can arise independently from each of these portions of the VNC motor neurons.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the double VNC/DNC cut experiments.

claims.claim: The A motor neurons are not required for body oscillation in VNC-lesioned worms.
claims.source: We severed the VNC and DNC in either one or two locations after ablating the A motor neurons with Punc-4::miniSOG. Animals in which the VNC and DNC had been severed near the head were capable of robust wave generation and propagation posterior to the head (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B). Animals in which the VNC and DNC were severed in two locations were capable of rhythmic activity in the mid-body or tail, although we did not observe any cases of simultaneous oscillation in each segment (N = 20 worms, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C). These results support the idea that the A motor neurons are not required for generation of rhythmic forward waves in surgically isolated segments of the VNC motor circuit.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claims.claim: The B motor neurons are required for rhythm generation in VNC-lesioned worms.
claims.source: To test this idea, we used VNC-lesioned worms in which the DA and DB motor neurons were ablated by miniSOG and the VB motor neurons were ablated by an infrared laser as before. After nerve cord surgery, worms in either B-ablation condition, like mock controls, were highly inactive. Application of a mechanical stimulus caused tight coiling, especially but not exclusively in the DB-only ablation condition (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C, Video 6). Despite this coiling, we observed at least one case of a VNC-lesioned, DB-ablated worm appearing to move the very tip of its tail, possibly in a rhythmic fashion, suggesting that DB neurons may not be required for rudimentary oscillation in at least the most posterior portion of the tail. However, in VNC-isolated worms for which most DB and VB neurons were ablated, we never observed rhythmic movements (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–F; N = 19 mechanical stimulus trials from nine worms). These results suggest that, as was the case for optogenetic 2FU, the B motor neurons are required for rhythm generation in VNC-lesioned worms.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C-F and Video 6.

claims.claim: Anterior VNC/DNC cuts disrupt normal head undulation.
claims.source: The observation that anterior VNC/DNC cuts disrupt normal head undulation (Figure 6A) suggests that rhythm generation by the head circuit may require inputs from the VNC.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Rhythm generation by the head circuit may require inputs from the VNC.
claims.source: The observation that anterior VNC/DNC cuts disrupt normal head undulation (Figure 6A) suggests that rhythm generation by the head circuit may require inputs from the VNC.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that head undulation is disrupted after VNC/DNC cuts.

claims.claim: Very slow head undulation was occasionally observed in animals with VNC/DNC cuts in two locations slightly more posterior to the head, indicating that head undulation is still possible under these conditions.
claims.source: However, we occasionally observed very slow head undulation in these animals, indicating that head undulation is still possible under these conditions (Figure 6D, Video 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D and Video 5.

claims.claim: Input from the posterior motor circuit may be essential for the normal frequency of head undulation.
claims.source: Another possibility is that input from the posterior motor circuit is essential for the normal frequency of head undulation. The latter hypothesis may be supported by our earlier observation that strong decoupling of head and tail oscillations by muscle ablation (i.e. without lesioning the nerve cord or parallel tracts) resulted in similarly slow head oscillations (Figure 3D), while weak decoupling resulted in moderately slower head oscillations (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by observations from Figures 3A and 3D.

claims.claim: The C. elegans forward locomotor circuitry possesses at least three units capable of independent oscillation, with two units located outside the head.
claims.source: These results suggest that the C. elegans forward locomotor circuitry possesses at least three units capable of independent oscillation, with two units located outside the head.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the VNC/DNC lesioning experiments.

claims.claim: Oscillations are possible in each segment when isolated from the others.
claims.source: Although we did not observe simultaneous three-frequency forward undulation in any animal tested, we have shown that oscillations are possible in each segment when isolated from the others.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: When the VNC and DNC were severed at any one of a number of different locations, undulations posterior to the damage arose near each cut location.
claims.source: When we severed the VNC and DNC at any one of a number of different locations (anterior to VB3, VB5, VB6, VB7, VB9, VB10, and VB11), we found that undulations posterior to the damage arose near each cut location (Figure 7B–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B-E.

claims.claim: Bending amplitude recovered just posterior to each cut location, rather than at a fixed body coordinate.
claims.source: Bending amplitude similarly recovered just posterior to each cut location, rather than at a fixed body coordinate (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: Oscillations in the tail usually had a higher frequency when the nerve cords were severed in the tail than when they were severed near the head.
claims.source: Oscillations in the tail usually had a higher frequency when the nerve cords were severed in the tail than when they were severed near the head (Figure 7G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7G.

claims.claim: The smallest VNC segment that produced clear and robust rhythmic waves was the region between VB9 and the tail.
claims.source: The smallest VNC segment that produced clear and robust rhythmic waves was the region between VB9 and the tail.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the systematic VNC/DNC severing experiments.

claims.claim: The most compact rhythm-generating unit of the forward motor circuit is at least as small as the region containing VB9, VB10, VB11, DB6, and DB7.
claims.source: These results suggest that the most compact rhythm-generating unit of the forward motor circuit is at least as small as the region containing VB9, VB10, VB11, DB6, and DB7.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that this region can generate rhythms when isolated.

claims.claim: During 2FU, head frequency decreases relative to the unperturbed swimming frequency.
claims.source: We found that during 2FU, head frequency decreases relative to the unperturbed swimming frequency (Figure 8A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: Slowing of head frequency was often even more dramatic when decoupling was stronger.
claims.source: Slowing was often even more dramatic when decoupling was stronger (Figures 3D and 6D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 3D and 6D.

claims.claim: Anteriorward coupling, in addition to posteriorward coupling, may be present in the forward locomotor circuitry.
claims.source: These observations suggest that anteriorward coupling, in addition to posteriorward coupling, may be present in the forward locomotor circuitry.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that head frequency decreases during 2FU.

claims.claim: Rhythmically inhibiting the mid-body BWMs caused worms to exhibit a head bending frequency approximately one half that of the imposed frequency.
claims.source: Worms subjected to this procedure exhibited a head bending frequency approximately one half that of the imposed frequency.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the rhythmic optogenetic inhibition experiments.

claims.claim: The factor of one half in the entrainment is likely due to the presence of two phases during the rhythmic locomotory cycle of any single part of the body during which the curvature is close to zero (i.e. muscles are relaxed).
claims.source: The factor of one half is likely due to the presence of two phases during the rhythmic locomotory cycle of any single part of the body during which the curvature is close to zero (i.e. muscles are relaxed).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed 1:2 entrainment ratio.

claims.claim: The head frequency could be entrained to a range of imposed mid-body frequencies.
claims.source: We found the head frequency could be entrained to a range of imposed mid-body frequencies. Subjecting body coordinates 33–66 to pulsed illumination at frequencies from approximately 1 to 2 Hz caused an increase in the power spectrum of the worm's oscillations at frequencies corresponding to half of the imposed frequency, and a decrease at other frequencies. Pulsing at frequencies below 1 Hz generally led to head oscillations near the imposed frequency (Figure 8C(ii)).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8C(ii).

claims.claim: A mid-body rhythmic signal can entrain head bending.
claims.source: These results show that a mid-body rhythmic signal can entrain head bending, and point to the presence of an anteriorward coupling mechanism within the motor circuit.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rhythmic optogenetic inhibition experiments.

claims.claim: There is an anteriorward coupling mechanism within the motor circuit.
claims.source: These results show that a mid-body rhythmic signal can entrain head bending, and point to the presence of an anteriorward coupling mechanism within the motor circuit.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the entrainment experiments.

claims.claim: Rhythmic optogenetic inhibition of the midbody cholinergic neurons caused worms to adjust their head bending frequency to match one-half of the imposed frequency.
claims.source: We applied a rhythmic optogenetic inhibition pattern to the midbody cholinergic neurons in Punc-17::NpHR worms. Once again, worms subject to this procedure quickly adjust their head bending frequency to match one-half of the imposed frequency (Figure 8D(i), Video 7).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8D(i) and Video 7.

claims.claim: Rhythmic illumination of the tail cholinergic neurons at 2 Hz increased the magnitude of head bending at 1 Hz.
claims.source: Moreover, rhythmic illumination of the tail cholinergic neurons at 2 Hz similarly increased the magnitude of head bending at 1 Hz (Figure 8D(ii)).

results.result: Posterior undulation persists despite anterior paralysis induced by optogenetic inhibition of muscles or neurons, or by physical lesioning. When the anterior 33% or 45% of the worm was paralyzed, robust oscillations were observed in posterior regions, and tail undulation frequency increased. This finding is consistent with a multi-oscillator model and inconsistent with a single oscillator model relying on reflex-like signaling for wave propagation.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C44 provide converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches (optogenetic inhibition of muscles, optogenetic inhibition of neurons, miniSOG-mediated muscle lesioning, and thermal lesioning) that posterior undulation can persist despite anterior paralysis. The data shown in Figures 2A-E and supplementary figures support these observations. The inference that this is consistent with a multi-oscillator model (C44) is logically sound given the experimental results.

results.result: The C. elegans forward motor circuit contains at least two units capable of independent rhythm generation. Optogenetic inhibition of neck muscles, cholinergic neurons, or B-type motor neurons resulted in two-frequency undulation (2FU), where the tail exhibited higher frequency oscillations than the head. 2FU was also observed after stronger disruption via muscle lesioning, selective activation of tail motor neurons, and in worms transitioning between regions of different viscosities without any internal perturbations.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C58 describe a series of experiments demonstrating 2FU under various conditions. The data in Figures 3A-F and supplementary figures support the occurrence of 2FU. The conclusion that the motor circuit contains at least two independent rhythm generators (C57) is well-supported by the multiple lines of evidence showing that posterior oscillations can occur at different frequencies than anterior oscillations when coupling is disrupted.

results.result: Most premotor interneurons, including PVC, are not essential for 2FU, but AVB may play a key role in activating the rhythm generator(s). Strains with ablated premotor interneurons (Pnmr-1::ICE and Pglr-1::ICE) and mutants lacking UNC-7/UNC-9 gap junctions were capable of 2FU during neck muscle inhibition. However, ablation of AVB nearly eliminated 2FU events.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C68 are supported by data shown in Figures 4A, 4B, 4E, and supplementary figures. The genetic ablation and mutant studies provide strong evidence that most premotor interneurons are not required for 2FU, while AVB appears to be important. The inference that AVB may activate the rhythm generator(s) (C68) is reasonable given the near elimination of 2FU after AVB ablation.

results.result: The A, VC, and D motor neurons are not required for 2FU. Ablation of A and VC motor neurons did not prevent 2FU, and unc-49 mutants (lacking functional D-type motor neuron output) were capable of 2FU. Ablation of individual B motor neurons or small subsets reduced but did not eliminate 2FU, suggesting that in the presence of premotor interneurons, the B class motor neurons contribute to 2FU, but no single member is essential. Posterior rhythm generation can arise from multiple subsets of B or AS motor neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C76 are supported by data in Figures 4C-F and supplementary figures. The systematic ablation studies provide strong evidence that A, VC, and D motor neurons are not required for 2FU, while B motor neurons contribute but are individually dispensable. The conclusion that multiple subsets of B or AS motor neurons can generate posterior rhythms (C76) is a reasonable inference from the data, though it is somewhat speculative.

results.result: The B motor neurons as a class are essential for independent tail undulation during forward movement. vab-7 mutants, in which DB motor neurons are disrupted, were incapable of 2FU. Elimination of most DB or most VB motor neurons sharply reduced but did not eliminate 2FU. However, when both DB and most VB motor neurons were removed, animals were completely incapable of 2FU (0 out of 102 trials).
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C83 are strongly supported by data in Figure 5 and supplementary figures. The systematic ablation of DB and VB motor neurons, culminating in the complete elimination of 2FU when both are removed, provides compelling evidence that the B motor neurons as a class are essential for independent tail undulation. The blinded, randomized scoring adds rigor to the assessment.

results.result: Multiple lesion-separated VNC segments are capable of independent rhythm generation. Severing the VNC and DNC posterior to the pharynx, with or without additional head lesioning, resulted in robust oscillations posterior to the cut, often at higher frequencies than the mid-body. When the VNC and DNC were cut in two locations (neck and tail), animals could generate robust oscillations posterior to each cut at different frequencies. These results suggest that the C. elegans forward locomotor circuitry possesses at least three units capable of independent oscillation, with two units located outside the head. The A motor neurons are not required, but the B motor neurons are required for rhythm generation in VNC-lesioned worms.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C103 describe VNC/DNC severing experiments and are supported by data in Figures 6A-E and supplementary figures. The observation that multiple isolated VNC segments can generate independent oscillations provides strong evidence for distributed rhythm generation. The conclusion that there are at least three oscillatory units (C102) is well-supported by the double-cut experiments. The requirement for B motor neurons (C97) is supported by supplementary data.

results.result: Undulations can arise in arbitrary portions of the VNC motor circuit. When the VNC and DNC were severed at various locations (anterior to VB3, VB5, VB6, VB7, VB9, VB10, and VB11), undulations arose near each cut location, and bending amplitude recovered just posterior to each cut. Oscillations in the tail had higher frequency when the nerve cords were severed in the tail than near the head. The smallest VNC segment that produced clear and robust rhythmic waves was the region between VB9 and the tail, suggesting that the most compact rhythm-generating unit is at least as small as the region containing VB9, VB10, VB11, DB6, and DB7.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C108 are supported by data in Figures 7B-G. The systematic severing of the VNC/DNC at different locations provides strong evidence that rhythm generation is distributed along the VNC. The identification of the smallest segment capable of generating rhythms (C107-C108) is a reasonable inference from the data, though the exact boundaries of the minimal unit remain somewhat uncertain.

results.result: Anteriorward coupling is present in the forward locomotor circuitry. During 2FU, head frequency decreases relative to unperturbed swimming, and this slowing is more dramatic with stronger decoupling. Rhythmically inhibiting mid-body BWMs, cholinergic neurons, or B motor neurons caused worms to exhibit head bending at approximately one-half the imposed frequency, demonstrating that a mid-body rhythmic signal can entrain head bending. This entrainment was observed over a range of imposed frequencies and suggests the presence of an anteriorward coupling mechanism, likely mediated neuronally by the VNC motor neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C120 describe rhythmic optogenetic entrainment experiments and are supported by data in Figures 8A-D and supplementary figures. The observation that head frequency decreases during 2FU (C109-C110) is well-documented. The rhythmic entrainment experiments (C112-C119) provide strong evidence for anteriorward coupling. The inference that this coupling is mediated neuronally by VNC motor neurons (C120) is reasonable given the various manipulations tested, though the exact mechanism remains speculative.

results.result: Rhythm generation by the head circuit may require inputs from the VNC. Anterior VNC/DNC cuts disrupt normal head undulation, though very slow head undulation was occasionally observed in animals with cuts slightly more posterior to the head. Input from the posterior motor circuit may be essential for the normal frequency of head undulation, as strong decoupling by muscle ablation resulted in similarly slow head oscillations.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C101 are based on observations in Figures 6A, 6D, 3A, and 3D. While the data show that head undulation is disrupted after VNC/DNC cuts (C98), the interpretation that the head circuit requires VNC inputs (C99) is speculative. The observation of occasional slow head undulation (C100) suggests that the head can generate rhythms independently, but at altered frequencies. The hypothesis that posterior input is essential for normal head frequency (C101) is plausible but not definitively proven, as alternative explanations (e.g., damage to parallel tracts) are acknowledged.

results.result: The results reveal a picture of forward locomotor control in C. elegans similar to that found in the lamprey and leech. Rhythmogenic capability is distributed along the VNC motor circuit, and is only detectable when coupling is disrupted. During locomotion, multiple rhythm generating units with different rhythmic properties are combined by strong inter-unit coupling to form one functional unit. The normal locomotory frequency is generally intermediate between the head and tail frequencies exhibited during 2FU. The C. elegans motor circuit is coupled by posteriorward proprioception and additional anteriorward and posteriorward coupling mechanisms, allowing the entire circuit to operate as one unit.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C142 synthesize the major findings and compare them to other organisms. The comparison to lamprey and leech (C129, C142) is supported by the cited literature (C121-C128) and the experimental results. The conclusions about distributed rhythmogenesis (C130-C131), multi-oscillator coupling (C135-C136), and bidirectional coupling (C140-C141) are well-supported by the data presented in the manuscript. These are integrative conclusions that tie together the various experimental results.

results.result: The cholinergic B and AS motor neurons are a likely source of posterior rhythmogenesis during C. elegans forward locomotion. Disruption or removal of most or all B motor neurons virtually abolished independent tail undulations, while elimination of other motor neurons and premotor interneurons did not. Stimulation of select B and AS neurons led to local, high-frequency oscillations. Imposing a rhythmic signal on mid-body B motor neurons entrained whole-body locomotor frequency, and the swimming phase was reset almost immediately after the first inhibitory stimulus. The B motor neurons are rhythmically active in phase with locomotion, satisfying key criteria for candidate oscillator neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C154 synthesize multiple lines of evidence implicating B and AS motor neurons in rhythm generation. The ablation studies (C148), stimulation experiments (C149), entrainment experiments (C150), and phase resetting observations (C152) provide converging support. The comparison to criteria used in leech studies (C153-C154) strengthens the argument. While the exact mechanism of rhythm generation remains unclear, the evidence strongly implicates B motor neurons as key components.

results.result: A new working model of C. elegans forward locomotion is proposed with three oscillator units: an unknown head CPG, the VNC motor neurons between VB3 and AS7, and the VNC motor neurons between VB9 and AS11. The two VNC units are justified by data from worms with multiple VNC/DNC cuts. AS is included because it has not been directly investigated and could be important for tail rhythm generation. The premotor interneurons, especially AVB, are important for activating the oscillatory circuit and may have additional roles. When the VNC and DNC were severed at arbitrary locations, oscillations resumed posterior to each cut over a wide range of circuit sizes, and even smaller circuit units, perhaps individual motor neurons, may be capable of generating rhythmic outputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C173-C178 present a working model based on the experimental results. The model is supported by data from Figures 6C, 7, and other experiments. The inclusion of three oscillator units (C173-C174) is justified by the double-cut experiments. The inclusion of AS (C175) is speculative but reasonable given the lack of investigation. The role of premotor interneurons (C176) is supported by the ablation studies. The observation that oscillations can arise from various VNC segments (C177) is well-documented. The speculation about even smaller units (C178) is appropriately cautious. Overall, the model is a reasonable synthesis of the data, though some aspects remain speculative.

results.result: C. elegans is a tractable model organism for studying locomotion. It has a compact nervous system with a few hundred neurons and a nearly complete wiring diagram. Its optical transparency allows monitoring of neural activity and optogenetic manipulation. It is amenable to genetic manipulations and shares genetic homology with humans. The locomotor circuit consists of interneurons, excitatory and inhibitory motor neurons (A, B, VC, D, AS types), and body wall muscles, with most motor neuron cell bodies located in the VNC. A-type neurons are essential for reverse locomotion, B-type for forward locomotion, and D-type for normal bending amplitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C17 provide background information about C. elegans as a model organism and the basic architecture of its locomotor circuit. These claims are well-established in the field and are supported by the cited references (White et al., 1986; Chalfie et al., 1985; McIntire et al., 1993b; etc.). This is foundational knowledge that sets the stage for the experimental work.

results.result: Prior work has established that the identity of the rhythmic generator(s) for C. elegans forward locomotion is unknown, and it is unclear how many such generators exist. Worms are capable of limited movement despite ablation of most premotor interneurons, and forward locomotion was observed after ablation of all premotor interneurons and A motor neurons. Sensory feedback plays an important role in coordinating motor behavior, and computational models based on proprioceptive feedback have recapitulated key aspects of locomotion. A single-oscillator model with proprioceptive coupling has been proposed, but alternative multi-oscillator models are also possible.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C35 summarize prior work and the motivation for the current study. These claims are supported by the cited references (Chalfie et al., 1985; Kawano et al., 2011; Gao et al., 2017; Wen et al., 2012; etc.). The description of the single-oscillator model (C29-C32) and the alternative multi-oscillator model (C34-C35) accurately represents the state of the field and sets up the key question addressed by the manuscript.

results.result: Illuminating body coordinates 50–65 in Pmyo-3::NpHR worms caused substantial paralysis in the tail, consistent with previous findings.
results.evaluation: Claim C36 is a control experiment confirming that the optogenetic system works as expected in the posterior, consistent with prior studies (Leifer et al., 2011; Wen et al., 2012). This validates the experimental approach.

results.evaluation: Claim C52 is a speculative interpretation of the observed inverse relationship between amplitude and frequency. While the observation is supported by data (C51), the proposed explanation is not directly tested and remains a hypothesis.

results.result: Almost all synaptic connections to the VNC motor neurons are made by the premotor interneuron classes AVB, PVC, AVA, AVD, and AVE. Laser ablation studies have indicated that AVB, and to a lesser degree PVC, are essential for normal forward locomotion, although rudimentary forward crawling is possible in their absence if the A motor neurons are also removed.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C61 summarize prior work on premotor interneurons, supported by citations to White et al., 1986; Chalfie et al., 1985; and Gao et al., 2017. This provides context for the genetic ablation experiments.

results.result: In zebrafish, lampreys, and leeches, rhythmogenic capability for swimming undulations is distributed along the spinal cord or VNC. Isolated segments can generate oscillations, but in the intact animal, intersegmental coupling drives the system to adopt a single locomotor frequency. In the leech, the most robustly oscillating ganglia are in the middle of the body, and isolated midbody ganglia have higher frequency than those near the head or tail.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C128 summarize prior work on other organisms, supported by citations to Kiehn, 2006; Mullins et al., 2011; Cohen, 1987; Pearce and Friesen, 1985; Kristan et al., 2005. This provides comparative context for interpreting the C. elegans results.

results.result: In the leech, oscillatory interneurons mediate bidirectional coupling between midbody ganglia, and coupling results from a mixture of proprioceptive feedback and central control. Injection of sinusoidally varying current into leech stretch receptor cells was sufficient to entrain swimming activity. Imposed rhythmic movements are also capable of entraining fictive swimming in isolated preparations of the lamprey spinal cord and other systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C146 summarize prior work on coupling mechanisms in other organisms, supported by citations to Friesen and Hocker, 2001; Kristan et al., 2005; Yu et al., 1999; Yu and Friesen, 2004; Grillner et al., 1981; McClellan and Sigvardt, 1988; and others. This provides context for the entrainment experiments in C. elegans.

results.result: Descriptions of swimming CPGs in vertebrates have tended to exclude motor neurons as members of the CPG, with most oscillatory function attributed to interneurons. However, leech inhibitory motor neurons are ascribed a role in swimming rhythm generation, motor neurons comprise the crab stomatogastric CPG, and recent work has shown that motor neurons are key components of several locomotory pattern generators. In zebrafish, motor neurons for swimming are bidirectionally coupled to locomotion-driving interneurons and influence their activity. There is a growing recognition that motor neurons may themselves participate in rhythm generation.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C163 summarize the evolving understanding of motor neuron roles in rhythm generation across various organisms, supported by citations to Kiehn, 2016; Kristan et al., 2005; Mullins et al., 2011; Marder and Bucher, 2007; Rotstein et al., 2017; Song et al., 2016. This provides context for the finding that B motor neurons may be rhythm generators in C. elegans.

results.result: When the VNC and DNC of C. elegans were severed, independent, higher frequency undulations occurred posterior to the severed region, unlike in leeches where VNC disruption did not prevent wave propagation. However, severing VNC intersegmental coordinating neurons in in vitro leech preparations induced uncoordinated oscillations. The laser lesioning of the VNC likely did not remove severed processes of premotor interneurons or prevent nonsynaptic neurotransmission. When the VNC was isolated from the head ganglia, rhythmic tail undulation was reliably evoked by mechanical stimulus, but independent tail undulations were rare after ablating AVB. The AVB processes that remain in severed VNC segments may continue to provide excitation to B motor neurons. The observation that tail undulation was reliably evoked after eliminating all synaptic inputs from the head is inconsistent with the notion that independent oscillations require synaptic input from head circuitry.
results.evaluation: Claims C164-C172 discuss differences between C. elegans and leech VNC severing results, and address the apparent discrepancy between VNC severing and AVB ablation experiments. The observations are supported by data in Figures 6 and 7, and the discussion acknowledges limitations of the methods (C167-C168). The proposed explanation involving remaining AVB processes (C171) is speculative but reasonable. The conclusion that synaptic inputs from the head are not required (C172) is supported by the VNC severing data.

results.result: The finding that the architecture for rhythm generation in C. elegans locomotion shares key properties with other vertebrate and invertebrate models sets the stage for molecular, cellular, and network-level investigations of motor coordination in a uniquely tractable model organism.
results.evaluation: Claim C179 is a concluding statement about the significance of the findings. It is supported by the overall results of the study, which demonstrate that C. elegans has a distributed rhythm-generating architecture similar to other organisms, combined with the well-established advantages of C. elegans as a model system.
